```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", echo = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.6, dpi = 96, out.width = "100%"
)
library(ggplot2)
b7 <- readRDS("data/bench_097.rds")
b6 <- readRDS("data/bench_096.rds")
pr <- readRDS("data/bench_097_probe.rds")
ag <- readRDS("data/agreement_results.rds")
sess <- attr(b7, "session")
bb <- rbind(b7, b6)
tm <- function(ver, meth, nn) bb[bb$version == ver & bb$method == meth & bb$n == nn, "median_s"]
pget <- function(m, nn, col) pr[pr$method == m & pr$n == nn, col]
```

Several R packages compute silhouette widths. This article sets out what each
one computes, how long **Silhouette** and the alternatives take and how much
memory they need as the number of observations grows, and how closely the
simplified widths of **Silhouette** agree with the classical widths. The
results are cached; the scripts that produced them are in
[`data-raw/benchmarks`](https://github.com/kskbhat/Silhouette/tree/main/data-raw/benchmarks)
in the package repository.

# What each package computes

| Capability | In **Silhouette** | In **cluster**, **factoextra**, **fclust** or **bluster** |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Classical widths from all pairwise dissimilarities | not computed; `plotSilhouette()` draws them | `cluster::silhouette()`, and in `pam()`, `clara()` and `fanny()`; `fclust::SIL()`; **factoextra** through **cluster** |
| Approximate classical widths in linear time | none | `bluster::approxSilhouette()` |
| Simplified widths from distances or similarities to each cluster | `Silhouette()`, medoid and PAC | none |
| Widths from membership or posterior probabilities | `softSilhouette()`, `cerSilhouette()`, `dbSilhouette()` | none |
| Membership-weighted (fuzzy) average | `average = "fuzzy"` for every width | `fclust::SIL.F()`, on classical widths |
| Extended silhouette for multi-way partitions | `extSilhouette()` | none |
| Silhouette plot | `plotSilhouette()` (**ggplot2**), also for results of **cluster**, **factoextra** and **drclust** | `factoextra::fviz_silhouette()` (**ggplot2**); `plot()` in **cluster** (base graphics) |
| Input stored | an $n \times K$ matrix | $n(n-1)/2$ dissimilarities (**cluster**, **factoextra**, **fclust**); the $n \times p$ data (**bluster**) |

The classical silhouette of @rousseeuw1987silhouettes compares each
observation's average dissimilarity to the members of its own cluster with its
average dissimilarity to the members of the nearest other cluster.
`bluster::approxSilhouette()` [@bluster] replaces those averages with
root-mean-squared distances, which it can compute from the cluster centroids;
it is designed for crisp partitions of Euclidean data. **Silhouette** instead
compares distances (or similarities) to a representative of each cluster
[@vanderlaan2003pam], or membership probabilities, so any $n \times K$ matrix
will do: distances to medoids under any dissimilarity, dynamic time warping
distances to time-series prototypes, or the posterior probabilities of a
mixture model. The widths therefore differ from the classical widths, as the
last section shows.

# Time and memory

We timed each computation end to end, from the data and the fitted partition
to the average width, so that each method pays for building its own input:

```{r timed-exprs, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
# cluster: classical widths from the n x n distances
D <- stats::dist(X); summary(cluster::silhouette(cl, D))$avg.width
# Silhouette: simplified widths from the n x K distances to the centers C
summary(Silhouette(proxy::dist(X, C)), print.summary = FALSE)$avg.width
# bluster: approximate classical widths
mean(bluster::approxSilhouette(X, cl)$width)
# fclust: fuzzy silhouette of Campello and Hruschka on classical widths
fclust::SIL.F(X, U, alpha = 2)
```

The data were five-dimensional Gaussian mixtures with $K = 5$
well-separated components; `cl` was the k-means partition, `C` its centers and
`U` memberships of fuzzy c-means form. Times are medians over 10 repetitions
for $n \le 10\,000$ and 3 above, measured with **bench** on one core of an
Intel Xeon processor at `r sub(".*@ *([0-9.]+) *GHz.*", "\\1", sess$cpu)` GHz
with 8 GB of memory, running `r sess$R` on
`r sub('^PRETTY_NAME="?([^"]*)"?$', "\\1", attr(b7, "environment")$os_release)`
with the reference BLAS and LAPACK. Both versions were timed on the same machine;
the results store `sessionInfo()`, the BLAS and LAPACK libraries and the tested
source. The timings are conditional on this design and machine: they show how
the costs grow with $n$, not a general ranking of the packages.

```{r fig-time, fig.alt = "Log-log line chart of time against n from 1,000 to 200,000. Silhouette 0.9.7 and bluster stay below about 0.2 seconds; Silhouette 0.9.6 rises linearly to about 14 seconds; cluster::silhouette rises quadratically to about 2 seconds at n = 10,000; fclust is the slowest."}
lab <- c(simplified_crisp = "Silhouette() 0.9.7", approx_bluster = "bluster::approxSilhouette()",
         rousseeuw_cluster = "cluster::silhouette()", fuzzy_fclust = "fclust::SIL.F()")
d7 <- b7[b7$method %in% names(lab), ]
d7$series <- lab[d7$method]
d6 <- b6[b6$method == "simplified_crisp", ]
d6$series <- "Silhouette() 0.9.6"
dd <- rbind(d7, d6)
dd$series <- factor(dd$series, c("Silhouette() 0.9.7", "Silhouette() 0.9.6",
                                 "bluster::approxSilhouette()", "cluster::silhouette()",
                                 "fclust::SIL.F()"))
ggplot(dd, aes(n, median_s, colour = series, shape = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1e3, 1e4, 1e5), labels = c("1,000", "10,000", "100,000")) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = function(x) format(x, scientific = FALSE, drop0trailing = TRUE, trim = TRUE)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#8fb8ea", "#1f9d74", "#eb6834", "#b8457e"), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15, 18, 8), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Number of observations n (log scale)", y = "Time (seconds, log scale)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

At $n = 10\,000$ the classical computation with **cluster** took
`r sprintf("%.2f", tm("0.9.7", "rousseeuw_cluster", 1e4))` seconds and
`fclust::SIL.F()` took `r sprintf("%.1f", tm("0.9.7", "fuzzy_fclust", 1e4))`
seconds, against `r sprintf("%.3f", tm("0.9.7", "simplified_crisp", 1e4))`
seconds for `Silhouette()`. The vectorized code of version 0.9.7 needed
`r sprintf("%.2f", tm("0.9.7", "simplified_crisp", 2e5))` seconds at
$n = 200\,000$, where version 0.9.6 needed
`r sprintf("%.1f", tm("0.9.6", "simplified_crisp", 2e5))` seconds for identical
widths. Fuzzy averaging and the widths from membership probabilities cost about
the same as the crisp computation.

Memory was measured separately, by running each computation once in a fresh R
process and recording the increase in its peak resident memory. The classical
computation was attempted at every size in this way.

```{r tab-time}
tn <- c(1000, 5000, 10000, 20000, 25000, 50000, 1e5, 2e5)
ft <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "", ifelse(x < 0.01, sprintf("%.3f", x),
                  ifelse(x < 1, sprintf("%.2f", x), ifelse(x < 10, sprintf("%.1f", x), sprintf("%.0f", x)))))
fm <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "", ifelse(x < 1, "<1 MB",
                  ifelse(x < 1000, sprintf("%.0f MB", x), sprintf("%.1f GB", x / 1024))))
fb <- function(b) ifelse(b < 1e6, sprintf("%.0f kB", b / 1e3),
                  ifelse(b < 1e9, sprintf("%.0f MB", b / 1e6),
                         ifelse(b < 9.95e9, sprintf("%.1f GB", b / 1e9), sprintf("%.0f GB", b / 1e9))))
nlab <- format(tn, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
cls <- sapply(tn, function(nn) pget("classical", nn, "status"))
fail <- ifelse(cls == "killed", "killed", "fails")
t_cl <- sapply(tn, function(nn) {
  v <- tm("0.9.7", "rousseeuw_cluster", nn); if (length(v)) v else pget("classical", nn, "elapsed_s")
})
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  n = nlab,
  cluster = ifelse(cls == "ok", ft(t_cl), fail),
  Silhouette = ft(sapply(tn, function(nn) tm("0.9.7", "simplified_crisp", nn))),
  bluster = ft(sapply(tn, function(nn) tm("0.9.7", "approx_bluster", nn)))),
  align = "r", caption = "Time in seconds (medians).")
```

```{r tab-memory}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  n = nlab,
  cluster = ifelse(cls == "ok", fm(sapply(tn, function(nn) pget("classical", nn, "peak_MB"))), fail),
  Silhouette = fm(sapply(tn, function(nn) pget("silhouette", nn, "peak_MB"))),
  bluster = fm(sapply(tn, function(nn) pget("bluster", nn, "peak_MB"))),
  dist = fb(tn * (tn - 1) / 2 * 8),
  nK = fb(tn * 5 * 8)),
  align = "r", col.names = c("n", "cluster", "Silhouette", "bluster",
                             "size of dist object", "size of n x K matrix"),
  caption = "Increase in peak memory, and the size of the input each approach stores.")
```

"<1 MB" means that the increase was absorbed by memory the R process had
already reserved. The last two columns give the size of the input each approach
stores. On the 8 GB test machine, the classical computation was killed by the
operating system at $n = 20\,000$ and $25\,000$, after R had built the 1.6 GB
and 2.5 GB `dist` objects;
from $n = 50\,000$ R could not allocate the `dist` object at all. Its storage
grows with $n^2$, so each doubling of $n$ quadruples it; the size at which it
fails depends on the machine, but not the growth.

For crisp partitions, `Silhouette()` and `bluster::approxSilhouette()` both
scale linearly and both run in well under a second at $n = 200\,000$, so speed
and memory do not decide between them. What decides is the input, and how close
the result should be to the classical widths.

# Agreement with the classical silhouette

```{r agree-prep}
ag$same_med <- ag$k_rousseeuw == ag$k_medoid
ag$same_pac <- ag$k_rousseeuw == ag$k_pac
ag$same_bl <- ag$k_rousseeuw == ag$k_bluster
ag$diff_med <- ag$asw_medoid - ag$asw_rousseeuw
ag$diff_pac <- ag$asw_pac - ag$asw_rousseeuw
ag$diff_bl <- ag$asw_bluster - ag$asw_rousseeuw
agg <- aggregate(cbind(cor_widths, cor_bluster, diff_med, diff_pac, diff_bl,
                       same_med, same_pac, same_bl) ~ BarOmega + p, data = ag, FUN = mean)
agg <- agg[order(agg$p, agg$BarOmega), ]
reps <- nrow(ag) / nrow(agg)
rec <- c(classical = mean(ag$k_rousseeuw == ag$K), medoid = mean(ag$k_medoid == ag$K),
         pac = mean(ag$k_pac == ag$K), bluster = mean(ag$k_bluster == ag$K))
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
```

We simulated `r reps` data sets for each of six settings with **MixSim**:
$n = 500$, four elliptical Gaussian components with equal mixing proportions,
dimension $p \in \{2, 5\}$ and average
overlap $\bar\omega \in \{0.001, 0.01, 0.05\}$. For each data set we fitted
k-means for $K = 2, \dots, 8$ and computed the classical average width from
all pairwise distances, the medoid and PAC averages of `Silhouette()` from the
distances to the centroids, and the approximation of
`bluster::approxSilhouette()`.

```{r tab-agree}
f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%+.3f", round(x, 3) + 0)
setting <- data.frame(p = agg$p, overlap = format(agg$BarOmega, scientific = FALSE))
knitr::kable(cbind(setting,
  r_med = sprintf("%.3f", agg$cor_widths), r_bl = sprintf("%.3f", agg$cor_bluster),
  d_med = f3(agg$diff_med), d_pac = f3(agg$diff_pac), d_bl = f3(agg$diff_bl)),
  align = "r", col.names = c("p", "overlap", "r, medoid", "r, bluster",
                             "difference, medoid", "difference, PAC", "difference, bluster"),
  caption = "Correlation with the classical widths and difference from the classical average, at K = 4.")
knitr::kable(cbind(setting,
  s_med = pct(agg$same_med), s_pac = pct(agg$same_pac), s_bl = pct(agg$same_bl)),
  align = "r", col.names = c("p", "overlap", "medoid", "PAC", "bluster"),
  caption = "Share of data sets in which the average peaks at the same K as the classical average.")
```

Here *r* is the mean correlation between the individual widths and the
classical widths at the true $K = 4$, and the difference is the mean difference
between the average width and the classical average at $K = 4$.

```{r agree-values}
rc <- range(agg$cor_widths); rd <- range(agg$diff_med); rs <- range(agg$same_med)
rcb <- range(agg$cor_bluster); rdb <- range(agg$diff_bl); rsb <- range(agg$same_bl)
rsp <- range(agg$same_pac)
```

The simplified medoid widths rank observations much as the classical widths do
(correlations `r sprintf("%.2f", rc[1])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", rc[2])`), and
their average peaks at the same $K$ as the classical average in
`r pct(rs[1])` to `r pct(rs[2])` of data sets (PAC: `r pct(rsp[1])` to
`r pct(rsp[2])`). Their level is higher, by `r sprintf("%.2f", rd[1])` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", rd[2])`, because the distance to a centroid is smaller than
the average distance to all members of a cluster; the PAC average is close to
the classical level. Simplified averages should therefore not be compared with
classical averages or with thresholds published for them.

The **bluster** approximation is much closer to the classical widths:
correlations `r sprintf("%.3f", rcb[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", rcb[2])`, an
average `r sprintf("%.3f", -rdb[2])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", -rdb[1])` below the
classical one, and the
same $K$ in `r pct(rsb[1])` to `r pct(rsb[2])` of data sets. It achieves this by
accounting for the spread of each cluster, which the distance to a
representative ignores.

With `r reps` data sets per setting, these shares carry Monte Carlo error: the
95% interval around 92% runs from about 81% to 97%, so differences of a few
points between settings or methods are within simulation variability.

Three further settings, each with `r reps` data sets at overlap 0.01, check less
regular data: unequal cluster sizes (smallest mixing proportion 0.05), $p = 10$,
and 5% outliers.

```{r tab-agree-extra}
ax <- readRDS("data/agreement_extra.rds")
ax$same_med <- ax$k_rousseeuw == ax$k_medoid
ax$same_pac <- ax$k_rousseeuw == ax$k_pac
ax$same_bl <- ax$k_rousseeuw == ax$k_bluster
axg <- aggregate(cbind(cor_widths, cor_bluster, same_med, same_pac, same_bl) ~ setting,
                 data = ax, FUN = mean)
axg <- axg[match(c("unequal", "p10", "outliers"), axg$setting), ]
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  setting = c("unequal sizes", "p = 10", "5% outliers"),
  r_med = sprintf("%.3f", axg$cor_widths), r_bl = sprintf("%.3f", axg$cor_bluster),
  s_med = pct(axg$same_med), s_pac = pct(axg$same_pac), s_bl = pct(axg$same_bl)),
  align = "r", col.names = c("setting", "r, medoid", "r, bluster",
                             "same K, medoid", "same K, PAC", "same K, bluster"),
  caption = "Agreement with the classical silhouette in the three further settings.")
```

The conclusions carry over, although agreement on $K$ is lowest for the PAC
average with outliers. They are limited to what was simulated: Gaussian
mixtures with four components, $n = 500$, at most ten dimensions, k-means
partitions and Euclidean distances.

No index recovered the true $K = 4$ reliably in these settings: the classical
average did so in `r pct(rec["classical"])` of data sets, the medoid and PAC
averages in `r pct(rec["medoid"])` and `r pct(rec["pac"])`, and the **bluster**
average in `r pct(rec["bluster"])`. The silhouette, simplified or not, favors
compact, well-separated groups rather than the components of an elliptical
mixture.

# Which to use

- **The classical widths of a crisp partition.** Use `cluster::silhouette()`
  while the $n(n-1)/2$ dissimilarities fit in memory, and
  `bluster::approxSilhouette()` for Euclidean data beyond that.
  `plotSilhouette()` draws either result; see [Silhouette plots](plotting.html).
- **Soft and model-based clusterings.** Use `softSilhouette()`,
  `cerSilhouette()` or `dbSilhouette()` on the membership or posterior
  probabilities, or `Silhouette()` with `prob_matrix` on distances to the
  cluster centers; see `vignette("soft-clustering", package = "Silhouette")`.
- **Proximities to cluster representatives that are not Euclidean distances to
  centroids**, such as medoid dissimilarities or time-series distances to
  prototypes. Use `Silhouette()`.
- **Block and multi-way partitions.** Use `extSilhouette()` on the mode-wise
  results; see `vignette("multiway", package = "Silhouette")`.
- **The fuzzy silhouette of @campello2006fuzzy on classical widths.** Use
  `fclust::SIL.F()` for moderate $n$, or `average = "fuzzy"` in **Silhouette**
  for the same weighting of simplified widths.

# Reproducing the results

The scripts are in
[`data-raw/benchmarks`](https://github.com/kskbhat/Silhouette/tree/main/data-raw/benchmarks),
with instructions in its `README.md`. The memory probes read
`/proc/self/status` and so need Linux. The cached results record the machine
they ran on:

```{r machine, echo = TRUE}
str(attr(readRDS("data/bench_097.rds"), "session"))
```
